demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I acted in ways that go against who I am
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another person. 'Memory Feels Alien' can occur in PTSD, but paired with the available appraisal pattern it suggests stronger dissociation/self-detachment than is otherwise represented; more importantly, the memory cluster centers on fragmented visual recall and rage, whereas the appraisal cluster centers on guilt/meaning plus personal bodily damage, making the profile feel pulled between different trauma experiences.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type, which is causing serious injury to another person rather than being physically injured oneself. Unless the event also seriously injured the patient, this item is clinically implausible. It also does not fit well with the Memory → Negative Appraisals formulation, because the memory items provided more naturally support guilt, shame, or moral injury appraisals such as 'Violated Values' rather than permanent bodily damage.

vignette: At 52, Ajay had spent most of his adult life tending to the homes of others, sweeping floors and wiping counters in a high-rise apartment complex that housed a diverse mix of tenants. He had grown up in a modest South Asian family in New Jersey, and the pride he felt in keeping his work clean and orderly was a core part of his identity. The day he had come to work at the unit of an elderly man with arthritis, a sudden misstep while balancing a heavy bucket of bleach on a narrow corridor caused the man to stumble. The man fell onto the floor, his head striking the edge of the counter, and Ajay watched in horror as the man's face twisted in pain. The man lay still for a moment, his eyes wide, and Ajay felt an instant, jarring awareness of how his own small slip could lead to such suffering. The event was brief-just a few seconds-yet it became a mental snapshot that he could recall in vivid detail: the clink of the bucket, the man's gasp, the metallic taste of blood, the silence that followed. This picture would later flash before him unbidden whenever a loud clatter of a mop or the hiss of a cleaning solution entered his environment. In the weeks after the incident, Ajay began to experience intense rage whenever he tried to recall the moment. The picture in his mind was not a passive image; it was an eruption of anger directed at himself, as if the memory were a mirror holding him up to his own flaws. "I was so careless," he would think, "I let my life slip away." The recollection also triggered a cascade of self-blame: he was certain that the accident had been inevitable because of the way he had been careless. He felt a sudden, deep loss of meaning in his work; the routine task of cleaning became a reminder of the harm he could cause. He started to believe that every gesture of service was now a potential threat, and he could no longer see the values of humility and compassion he once held dear as aligned with his actions. The shame he felt that night in his kitchen, hearing the clatter of a bottle, echoed across his days and turned even the most ordinary chores into a painful reminder that he had violated his own standards. The connection between the vivid memory of that moment and his spiraling negative appraisals was clear in Ajay's own mind. Each time he pictured the elderly man's face, the rage that rose within him amplified his sense of guilt and helplessness. He came to believe that because he had acted in a way that was contrary to his self-image, he had doomed himself to a life of emptiness. The memory thus became the engine that pushed his negative self-appraisal further: the anger he felt upon recalling the event was inseparable from the sense that his life had lost its purpose, from the conviction that he had violated his own values, and from the painful self-blame that the accident was his fault. These thoughts, in turn, made it difficult for him to focus on the tasks that had once felt meaningful. Ajay's avoidance grew gradually. He would leave early from work on days when the apartment smelled of bleach or when the sound of someone saying "be careful" rang in his ears. He stopped chatting with his coworkers, fearing that a casual remark would trigger the flashback. His relationships outside of work suffered too; he no longer attended his daughter's school play, believing that the attention of others could pull him back into the memory. He also stopped volunteering at the community center, a role that had once given him a sense of purpose. The cumulative effect was a deepening isolation and a sense that nothing he did had meaning. When Ajay finally decided to seek help, he did so after a night of waking up in a panic at 2 a.m., the memory of the elderly man's fall replaying in his mind. He was afraid of losing his job and of the possibility that his anger might flare again, perhaps even at a loved one. He hoped to regain the sense of purpose he had lost and to find a way to reconcile his self-image with the painful reality of the accident. In therapy, he began to work through the memory, learning to observe it without the rage that had once consumed him, and to re-connect with the values that had guided his life before the accident.
